item.title: Christian-Based Counseling in Texas: Keys to Success
item.description:
Everyone strives for success, at least in one area of their lives or another, and Christian-based counseling in Texas can help. Some might consider success to be measured by the numbers in their bank account, and some might say that they’ll be a success when they hit a certain number of friends or followers on social media.

Others strive for prestige or social status in their community, aspiring to be a member of a certain social circle or club. Christians or religious people might define success differently, saying true success comes from laying down your life for others or following a preset career path in ministry.

No matter how you define success, chances are great that you’re striving for it. You may even be frustrated at the elusive nature of your goals. Success, even if it seems out of your grasp, is achievable if you embrace a few key concepts. While circumstances and opportunities vary, these principles consistently increase the likelihood of meaningful success.

Curiosity Leads to Success

Curiosity is not always celebrated in our culture. Think of all the mischief Curious George got into just because of his curiosity. The curious neighbor is often portrayed as the local gossip in popular media, and kids are sometimes told not to ask so many questions when parents don’t want to talk about a subject.

While this seems to be the cultural narrative, viewing curiosity in a negative way is damaging. Curiosity is what leads to knowledge, new experiences, and eventually, success.

Children are naturally curious. They love to explore new places and try new things. Unfortunately, adulthood has a way of stymying that curiosity in most people. But when you allow yourself to stay curious into adulthood, you permit yourself to learn. That mindset shift can change everything in your life. Curious people ask better questions, notice opportunities that others might overlook, and are far more willing to try new things, even if it means risking failure.

Curiosity pushes you to grow and explore because your desire to understand is so overwhelming that it compels you to learn. This mindset turns you from being a stymied passive bystander into an active, engaged participant in your own life.

Humility Leads to Success

Humility is another important element on the road to success. Humility is often associated with relational success, but it also plays a part in being successful in other areas of your life as well. How does being humble affect your success in business, ministry, and education, outside of its relational value?

Being humble leads to asking questions. Curiosity creates the desire to learn, but humility is what allows you to admit that you still need to. If you already think you know it all, you’re not as likely to succumb to your own curiosity. You won’t ask questions or try to learn from others because your pride tells you that you don’t need to.

If you’re full of pride, you’re also less likely to take constructive criticism. Everyone, even those with mounds of experience and skill, can make mistakes. When these inevitable mistakes happen, you can either acknowledge them and accept the occasional correction or you can blame others or circumstances. When you don’t own up to your mistakes, you miss an opportunity to grow. Not only is it a part of the growth process, but humility is a vital part of the formula for success.

Discipline Leads to Success

Being curious and humble is necessary, but if you aren’t able to sustain them, they’ll do you little good. Discipline, or perhaps another way of thinking of it, consistency, is also a key element to success.

Being disciplined requires you to learn how to live in the uncomfortable. In a society that values comfort with pillow-top beds and instant microwavable meals, it can be off-putting to live without comforts. But if you want to succeed in life, you have to learn how to survive and eventually thrive when you would rather leave or change your situation.

When you consistently put one foot in front of the other, systematically going through the steps that will lead to success, you will eventually see progress. The unfortunate reality is that many people with great ability and skill falter because they’re not disciplined enough to stay the course when the path becomes uncomfortable.

Biblical Advice

The Bible, the ultimate authority for guiding believers, agrees with the value of curiosity, humility, and discipline.

Scripture implores you to seek understanding and wisdom. In other words, the Bible tells you to be curious. Proverbs 25 says, “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter; to search out a matter is the glory of kings.” (Proverbs 25:2, NIV)

This verse eloquently discusses the profound tension that exists between the mystery of the universe and the human drive to understand it. There are aspects of existence and complexities of the universe that provide you with the why behind your curiosity.

God’s glory to conceal acknowledges that these truths remain intentionally complex or hidden. But conversely, the glory of kings is where you come in. The glory lies in the diligent labor of investigating your world. This Scripture suggests that one of the highest human achievements is to peel back those unknown layers of obscurity through research and analysis.

This curiosity and pursuit of knowledge are honorable to God and are God-given traits. He doesn’t flinch at our questions or discourage us from knowledge. He invites us to seek Him instead, and this is the source of real wisdom.

Humility, too, is championed and provides a central theme throughout the Bible. James 4:10 reminds us that if you humble yourself before the Lord, He will lift you up. True success in God’s eyes isn’t found in pride or in self-promotion. It’s the recognition that you’re dependent on Him and that you’re willing to learn from others.

In 1 Corinthians 9:24-27, Paul compares the Christian life to a race that requires training and perseverance. In other words, discipline. Success, like the Christian life, isn’t achieved overnight but requires consistency and a willingness to stay committed even when it’s difficult and even when it’s uncomfortable.

Different Goals, Same Principles

While the principles of curiosity, humility, and discipline are universal, the success they produce can look different depending on your focus. Worldly success is often centered on the accumulation of wealth, status, or influence. It’s a destination-based success.

Biblical success is measured in the transformation of your heart and defines who you are. It looks even more closely at who you are becoming and who you belong to. It’s valued in stewardship. It is not in what you have but how you’re using what you’ve already been given.

Despite these different finish lines, the mechanics of the race remain identical. The same curiosity a CEO uses to innovate a project is the curiosity a believer uses to study the depths of Scripture. The same discipline an athlete uses to train for a marathon is the discipline a person uses to maintain a consistent prayer life or to break an ingrained habit.

God has given us a powerful toolkit that helps us live successfully both in our relationship with him and the world around us.

Christian-Based Counseling in Texas: Therapy Supports Success

True success is the integration of your outward actions with your internal dialogue. It’s the realization that “searching out a matter” includes searching out the why behind your anxiety or understanding why you can’t seem to overcome a certain behavior.

Therapy can be a useful tool to help you achieve success, both in worldly and spiritual terms. When you peel back the layers of your own life, you are using your curiosity to drive success. In therapy, you will learn how to develop a sense of curiosity and humility and how to be consistent, even when uncomfortable.

Call our office to discuss how Christian-based counseling in Texas can help you find your own keys to success.

item.title: Signs of Depression in Children We Often Ignore and How to Intervene
item.description:
Every parent will tell you that children do and say unexpected things. It’s not unusual for kids to have unpredictable mood swings occasionally, develop sudden, unexpected quirks seemingly out of nowhere, or have unique preferences when it comes to their daily routine.

Reacting to these things rationally can be challenging, but most often they are harmless and amusing. However, there are certain childhood behaviors that go overlooked by parents and teachers alike, which point to something more serious happening. These are signs of depression in children.

More Than Sadness

Unfortunately, children can experience depression. It happens more often than people realize, and often affects children more deeply than they can express. Unlike sadness, depression is not a passing emotion. It cannot be fixed by a trip to the toy shop or an extra hour of screen time. Depression in children, just as with adults, is not a mood; it is a mental state that persists until it is recognized and treated.

Childhood depression is almost always linked to the following experiences:

  • A death in the family or a major life change
  • Bullying or social problems
  • Learning difficulties or academic pressures
  • Conflict and stress at home
  • Abuse and adverse childhood experiences
  • Ongoing illness or disability
  • Genetics that predispose them to mental health challenges

There could be a combination of these reasons, or a unique situation that triggers depression in a child. There might be an underlying mood disorder or condition that requires long-term treatment, or the child might benefit from play therapy or mental health support. Only when you notice the signs of depression in children can you begin to intervene and prescribe treatment for them.

Common Signs of Depression in Children and How You Can Help

Depression affects a person’s feelings, mind, and body. The signs of depression in children, therefore, are shown in their emotions, in their habits and behaviors, and in their bodies. It’s easy to overlook these symptoms because they often blend with the typical growth patterns of many kids. Keep in mind that “all behavior has meaning” and can tell you something about your child if you are paying attention.

The best you can do as a parent is to take note of any behaviors or physical symptoms that seem unusual. Speak with a doctor or mental health expert if something is persistent, extreme, or concerning to you.

Loss of Interest in Hobbies

One of the first signs of depression in children is when they suddenly become disinterested in the things they used to enjoy. They might spend more time alone, do less of the things they used to love doing, and stop participating in social events. Their teacher might tell you that they have become withdrawn in class when they used to be an active participant.

They mustn’t feel forced to reconnect with friends or to engage more socially, as this will likely make them withdraw even more. As much as possible, avoid putting them in the spotlight when talking with them. Gently invite them into activities, and when you talk with them, get down on their level.

Children withdraw to feel safe, and they will only open up if they know you won’t threaten to dismantle their emotional safe space. Often, the more that you can have this conversation come up with a child in a “natural, organic, unforced manner, the more effective it will be. This can take some strategy on your part when bringing it up, but it is worth the effort.

Emotional Outbursts

Many children have temper tantrums and the occasional angry outburst. Children instinctively regulate their emotions differently from adults. However, the one thing both kids and adults have in common is how they hide their most vulnerable emotions behind anger.

Rather than open up about what is disturbing them, they will become irritable, guarded, and angry if pushed. While you need to intervene with their angry outbursts, you must consider what is behind them, particularly if your child was never as irritable or angry before.

This is another conversation that may take some strategizing on your part to bring it up casually and thoughtfully without as many pitfalls and defensiveness on their part (and yours!). A key here is PATIENCE. Make sure you are calm first before proceeding.

It’s clear that they are dysregulated and unhappy, so scolding and punishment will only make things worse. Try to avoid minimizing their emotions by saying things like “You’re fine.” Rather, show them that you see their struggle and still love them. People of any age will only open up when they feel safe and seen. The fastest way to make a safe space for someone is to reduce criticism and make predictable routines.

Talking Negatively About Themselves

Sometimes you need to listen for signs of depression in children. They sound like “I’ll never be able to do this,” or “I’m a bad kid, and no one wants to be my friend.” These statements are glimpses into their fears and doubts. Unfortunately, if you hear things like this and don’t challenge them, these thoughts become foundational truths for your kid and determine their self-esteem for years to come.

You must intervene gently. Always acknowledge how they feel before you affirm them, or else they will feel dismissed. You can say something like, “You don’t feel good enough for your friends, huh?” before telling them that they are.

They need a model for self-compassion, so show them what it looks like. “I also feel like I’m not good enough sometimes. I remind myself that I am, even if I don’t feel like it.” Then, shine some good vibes on them by saying, “That’s sure not how I see you. Tell me more about how you see yourself.”

Struggles Concentrating

Children spend the majority of their lives in school, and so this is naturally the most common place for signs of depression to appear. Their grades might start sliding, their attendance in class declining, and their teachers might start raising concerns. This is especially a red flag if they had never struggled academically before.

You are not alone as you confront depression in your child. Hopefully, your child’s teacher cares enough to help. Together, you can outline some ways to help your child at home and at school. You might have to reduce the pressure you are putting on them to succeed, and change your tactic to be more hands-on with homework.

The teacher might have ideas on how to help with keeping them organized and focused on the work so that they don’t fall any further behind. Even if you don’t really see it this way, it’s important that you let your child know that while you want them to always do their best academically, there are more important things than making straight A’s. This includes their happiness and well-being.

Their grades can be brought back up, but addressing their mental health struggles should take priority, for now. Most children will know if their parents or caregiver are just trying to hide their disappointment, which can be toxic. Talking about it with them will help clear the air and avoid the unspoken, unaddressed shame that the child will often already be feeling.

Depression doesn’t always show up in a child’s behavior at home and school. More often than not, these signs of depression in children appear with physical symptoms and changes in routine. These are easy to ignore because kids often have physical symptoms of one kind or another, and many kids struggle with ordinary routines.

Changes in Appetite

Some kids really struggle with eating. They might prefer certain foods or eat the same meal repetitively. Most of these habits are ordinary, even when they are annoying. However, when there are big changes in the way your child eats, you should pay attention.

Just like with adults, kids cope with depression by eating more, craving sugar, or going off food entirely. If they are struggling to eat, you can help by offering them their favorite foods more frequently, and if they are overeating, reduce the snacks and junk food as much as possible. If the struggles persist for more than a month, consult a pediatrician to rule out any medical issues.

Changes in Sleep Routine

Many kids struggle with sleep at some point. Whether it’s throwing a tantrum at bedtime or taking a million years to get ready in the morning, kids have a love-hate relationship with sleep. However, count it as a warning sign when they consistently have issues falling asleep or waking up, to the point that it affects their day and drains their energy.

Regardless of what they say or do, children thrive on routine and consistency. You can create a calming bedtime routine by reducing screen time an hour before bed and turning the lights down low in their bedroom. Consider replacing screen time with other activities like reading or drawing before bedtime.

In case it comes up, keep in mind that trading the iPad for the phone does not count as “adjusting screen time.” Adjust the temperature if possible, speak in calming voices, and rehearse nightly routines, such as brushing teeth and saying prayers. These things will not target depression, but they help children get the right amount of sleep by keeping routines, which greatly reduces the effects of depression.

If you suspect that your child is dealing with depression, please reach out. Our reception team can connect you with me or another counselor who can provide support to you as an individual, to your child, or to your family group. Please contact our online reception team or consult our online directory for more information.

item.title: Healthy Mind: 6 Life Changes That Are Also Good for the Soul
item.description:
When identifying what makes for a healthy mind, we could look to any number of psychological theories for an answer. However, each theory varies in what it believes are the core components of what makes one’s mind healthy. Some theories focus on emotional awareness, while others focus more on flexibility of thinking.

Before modern psychological theories were created, the Bible spoke about how to have a healthy mind. Philippians 4:8 tells us to think about things that are honorable, just, pure, and lovely. If we aren’t used to focusing our mind on such things, it takes time to create these habits that lead to a healthier mind. Changing ways that we think and behave can be especially difficult when some of the unhealthy habits we currently possess have been with us since we were young.

Throughout our lifetime, we can learn and incorporate unhealthy habits without even being aware. Habits such as negativity, people-pleasing, distrust of others, and perfectionism (to name a few) can have an unfavorable impact on how we see ourselves, other people, and the world around us. If we continue in these unhealthy habits for long periods of time, it can take a toll on our mental health and lead to issues such as depression and anxiety.

The Nature of Creating Healthy Habits

Take a moment to think back to a time when you tried to do something new that would benefit your life. Perhaps you tried eating healthier or exercising more regularly. Maybe you decided to spend less money and to put more money away for a rainy day. Maybe you tried to be less critical in a relationship and improve communication. Were you successful in forming new ways of behaving? If so, how long did it take before the new behaviors seemed automatic?

Researchers Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts, and Wardle conducted a study in 2009, concluding that it usually takes around sixty-six days before a new habit feels automatic. However, the time to create the new habit can vary widely (18-254 days) based on the complexity of the desired behavior, personal motivation, and the surrounding circumstances in which the person is trying to create the habit.

The good news is that the researchers also found that slipping up and missing a single day does not significantly harm the overall long-term success of creating a healthy habit (Lally et al.). In this article, we will look at six life changes that you can turn into habits that will contribute to a healthier mind as well as positively increase how you feel about yourself and others.

Remember that adopting new behaviors can be challenging, so you may want to pick one new habit to start at a time. Be kind and forgiving to yourself if you mess up because, even if you must start the new behavior again, it just reinforces to the mind that it’s worth doing.

Cultivate hope and optimism
The Cambridge English Dictionary defines optimism as “the quality of being full of hope and emphasizing the good parts of a situation, or a belief that something good will happen.” We have numerous ways of looking at the world with hopeful expectations. As a child, did you ever throw a penny into a wishing well, hoping the wish would come true? How about wishing upon a star or making a wish while blowing out birthday cake candles?

Some people believe that hope and optimism are lost once you become an adult with serious responsibilities. With this outlook, individuals can get into a habit of complaining about everything. Complaining can be contagious but hope and optimism can be contagious too. Researchers have found that both optimism and hope are related to greater happiness (Snyder, 2002; Carver & Scheier, 2014).

Optimism is often paired with hope, but they are not the same thing. Optimism is a general outlook that good rather than bad things will happen, while hope tends to be focused on something specific. Hope focused on a specific goal may make you more likely to succeed. This is what is called a self-fulfilling prophecy.

The way you think can drive your behavior to the point of success or defeat, depending on whether your thoughts are positive or negative. The cycle then begins. The more optimistic and hopeful you are, the more success you may see. This, in turn, can make a person more optimistic and hopeful in the future. The great thing about optimism and hope is that anyone can learn these skills by becoming more aware and incorporating them into their daily life.

Simple Ways to Practice Hope and Optimism

  • Look up quotes from inspiring people that foster a sense of optimism and hope. Here are some of my favorites:

“When the world says give up, hope whispers, try it one more time.” – H. Jackson Brown, Jr.

“Keep your face to the sunshine, and you cannot see the shadows.” – Helen Keller

“Whether you think you can, or you think you can’t, you’re right.” – Henry Ford

  • Every day for a week, catch yourself when you are complaining. Try to take the circumstances you are complaining about and find something positive about it.
  • Name a source of inspiration you have. It could be a person or something that provides a sense of purpose. Think about why you find them/it inspiring. Could you be someone else’s source of inspiration?

Practicing gratitude
Consider this quote from Joyce Meyer: “I’m not where I want to be, but thank God I’m not where I used to be.” This quote shows that we don’t have to have it all together to be thankful for the progress we have made.

Gratitude in our everyday lives helps us to value what we have and decrease the focus on what we don’t have. Learning to increase gratitude helps us to appreciate and savor those everyday events and experiences and can also increase satisfaction in relationships.

How do we begin to increase gratitude in our lives? Gratitude is not just something we identify at Thanksgiving or Christmas but needs to be a habit that we incorporate daily to reap the benefits. We all have things that we wish were different in our lives, but we also have numerous things for which we can be thankful.

Taking time to identify the small things that we are blessed with can help to begin a pattern of gratitude. Gratitude can also be displayed in how we appreciate others. When was the last time you thanked someone for something small that they did? Creating this habit of thanking people close to you for all the small things they do can help to develop a habit of gratitude.

Plus, you get the added benefit of having a more positive relationship with that person. Overall, gratitude is one of the easiest life changes that a person can incorporate and has the biggest social and personal payoff, contributing to a healthier mind.

Simple Ways to Practice Gratitude

  • Write a thank-you note to someone who has made a difference in your life. Explain to them what they have done and what this means to you.
  • Every day for a week, write down three things that happened during the day for which you are thankful.
  • Take a walk outside. Notice different things that you see, hear, smell, and touch. As you walk, name the things in your life for which you are grateful.

Develop an attitude of curiosity
The Cambridge English Dictionary defines Curiosity as “An eager wish or desire to acquire new information or investigate strange things.” When we think about curiosity, we might think of a child learning about the world around them or how researchers come to achieve scientific breakthroughs. However, developing an attitude of curiosity about the people that we interact with every day can help decrease conflict and develop an increased level of empathy.

We each have our own interpretations of life and how the world around us works. This is called our perspective. Our perspective is determined by many things. Our genetics, the temperament we are born with, our culture, and the experiences we have throughout life can all influence perspective.

A large part of our perspective develops during the early years of life and can be highly impacted by our early caregiving relationships. Our perspective is made up of good experiences, bad experiences, and everything in-between.

Often, we misinterpret a situation because we judge the circumstances by our own perspectives. Our brains are wired to scan for information we are familiar with that might explain what is going on in any given circumstance. The researchers at the HeartMath Institute (2019) found that we have emotional responses to our perceptions of events.

These emotional responses usually lead us to negatively judge people and situations. When we are hurt by others in those situations, we can become distrustful and feel as though we have to protect ourselves. These trust issues can spread and become part of our overall perspective of people. We put up emotional walls and begin to judge the intentions of others quickly, which leads to miscommunication and increased conflict.

It causes hurt to be continually passed on. To approach a situation without judgment takes practice and a desire to be curious about how others might view things differently than yourself. This is called “perspective taking.” This can be a challenge, since we never really know what others are thinking unless they tell us.

However, practicing perspective taking with an attitude of curiosity toward others can help cultivate a healthy mind. Having an attitude of curiosity can help decrease personal frustration, thus decreasing health-damaging cortisol levels. An attitude of curiosity can also help increase patience in yourself and strengthen your relationships.

Simple Ways to Practice Curiosity

  • Analyze the way you view others’ intentions. Are you always thinking that people are out to harm you?
  • Pick a person with whom you don’t agree on something. Try to describe the reasons why that person may think differently than you.
  • The next time you interact with someone from a different culture or geographic location than your own, ask them about their favorite thing about their culture or the place they are from.

Develop a Sense of Humor
What people find humorous can vary from person to person based on their perspective. But the fact is, people like to laugh and be entertained. After all, laughter increases social bonding and is contagious, spreading from person to person to lighten the mood. As we look around our world, we find that a lot of time, money, and effort are spent creating ways to make people laugh, such as through music, movies, and art.

There is something positive that happens in our brains when we experience humor. According to researchers at Harvard University (2010), the surprising characteristic of a joke causes parts of your brain to search for a recognizable pattern. When the punchline comes, the brain shifts from trying to process information to looking for an emotional response.

During this process, your brain releases chemicals called neurotransmitters that make you feel good. So, having a good, hearty laugh can result in positive results for the body. Laughter has been found to relieve tension, decrease pain and stress, enhance the experience of pleasure, boost the immune system, and help reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke (Harvard University). Laughter really is the best medicine.

Life can be unpredictable, not fair, and downright out of control at times. The difficulty lies in being able to laugh about a mistake we make, when a mishap occurs, or when life just isn’t rolling out how we expect. We usually can’t reverse what happens to us and, if we are alive and learning the lessons of life, we are going to make mistakes.

Humor can be a valuable way of coping when things do not go as expected. Being able to find humor in a tough situation can help lessen the negative impact that it has on your mood and decrease your stress.

Simple Ways to Practice Humor

  • The next time you are feeling down, set aside some time to watch a funny movie or watch your favorite comedian.
  • Describe a really awkward past moment in your life. Can you laugh about this today?
  • If aliens were to abduct you, describe three silly things you do that would make them send you back.
  • Next time you are struggling, exaggerate about how things might be worse. Coming up with silly ways that a situation could have gone can help you find some humor in your current circumstance.

Experience pleasure in a healthy way
Researchers have found that pleasure is an important part of healthy psychological functioning and well-being (Berridge & Kringelbach, 2015). In fact, anhedonia, which is a symptom of depression, is when a person has difficulty finding pleasure in anything they experience. You can imagine how this would cause psychological functioning to decrease.

On the other hand, some experiences of pleasure can lead to addictive behavior. Most people might agree that eating indulgent foods, winning money at a slot machine, or playing a thrilling video game can create pleasurable experiences, but too much of anything can become excessive and unhealthy.

When examining what things bring pleasure, people also find that helping a friend, solving a problem, creating something artistic, meeting a goal, appreciating nature, and engaging in calming prayer or worship also provide pleasurable experiences. Some people might even say that these latter kinds of pleasures are more valuable overall since they tend to be more lasting (Heathwood, 2013).

When pursued with a healthy balance, pleasure brings about appreciation, playfulness, sensuality, spontaneity, and a healthy focus on self-care (Huta, 2014). In fact, healthy pleasure is essential for self-care and can increase feelings of joy, comfort, and relaxation.

There is a skill used in psychology, created by Fred Bryant, called savoring that helps to enhance an appreciation for pleasure and to regulate emotional states. The skill of savoring is more than just feeling and enjoying pleasure. Savoring requires a person to put forth conscious, mindful awareness.

This allows a person to fully soak in and prolong an experience while appreciating the positive emotions they feel. Savoring can be used to experience pleasure related to things in the past, present, or future. The savoring of pleasurable experiences helps to combat negative emotions, which can lead to depression and anxiety.

Simple Ways to Practice Pleasure

  • Choose something new to try that you have never done before. Examples could be trying a new and strange type of food, engaging in a type of sport you have never tried, or researching a topic of interest that you know nothing about.
  • List at least three things you think are beautiful. Describe them and really focus on detail.
  • Name something that you used to love as a kid. Do it again, no matter how silly it may seem. If you can’t do it, then imagine what it was like when you were a kid. Remember how it made you feel.
  • Is there something pleasurable that you are doing in excess that is creating problems in your life? Create a plan about how you could use more moderation.

Create positive social interactions
Have you ever had a bad day that was completely turned around by someone just noticing you and being nice? How does it make you feel when someone walking by smiles and says, “Good morning?” Have you ever had someone pay for your order at a drive-thru? These are small behaviors that work reciprocally. This means that the receiver and the giver of the kindness both benefit.

Performing small acts, like opening the door for someone, smiling, being friendly to the person waiting on you in a store, and telling someone to have a nice day, are some of the easiest ways to change your mood. Even better, it begins to change the mood of the people around you, creating a more positive environment.

According to the Mental Health Foundation (2019), depression and anxiety are the most common mental health issues. Even though these issues are common, when we are experiencing depression or anxiety, we often think we are the only ones who feels this way. People that you interact with every day may also be feeling depressed and/or anxious. We don’t know who they are because we have all gotten good at hiding how we really feel.

Many people around us are lonely, grieving, scared, or feel forgotten. You may be feeling that way right now. Simply smiling and being kind to someone can make them feel seen, valued, and at ease.

At the same time, you can feel seen, valued, and at ease when the person reciprocates with a warm response. Incorporating positive social interactions into your everyday life can create an atmosphere of compassion and generosity, as well as help combat feelings of depression and anxiety.

Simple Ways to Practice Positive Social Interactions 

  • Do you have difficulty asking for help when you need it? How does it feel when you help someone? Find something small that you need help with and ask someone to help you. When the task is done, reflect on how it made you feel and how you think the other person felt.
  • In the morning, every day for a week, smile and say good morning to passers-by. What kind of reactions did you get? Do you think it helped increase your mood?
  • Try doing a random act of kindness for someone. Examples could be writing an encouraging message for someone in the office who may get overlooked for what they do. You could let someone with fewer groceries go in front of you in line at the store, pay for someone’s morning coffee, or when you ask someone how they are, really listen.
